title: Job
subtitle: A good man's suffering, his friends' answers, and the voice from the storm
lead: Job is the story of a good man who loses everything. In the land of Uz, somewhere east of Israel, lives Job, a man the book calls "wholehearted and upright" (1:1), rich in flocks and herds and the father of ten children. In the court of heaven the Accuser asks the LORD a sharp question: "Is it for no reason that Job fears God?" (1:9). The LORD lets him find out. In one day Job loses his animals, his servants and all his children; then his body breaks out in boils, and he sits in the ashes scraping his skin with a broken piece of pottery. Still he does not curse God. Three friends come to comfort him, and for seven days they sit with him in silence.

Then Job curses the day he was born, and a long debate in poetry begins. His friends Eliphaz, Bildad and Zophar insist that God is just, that the wicked suffer and the righteous thrive, and that Job should look for the sin behind his pain and turn back to God. Job insists that he is innocent, accuses God of treating him as an enemy, and demands a hearing. After three rounds of speeches, a poem asks where wisdom can be found, Job swears an oath that he has done no wrong, and a young man named Elihu speaks for six chapters. At last the LORD answers Job from the windstorm. He gives no reason for Job's suffering. Instead he shows Job the world he made, from the foundations of the earth to the wild donkey, the ostrich, Behemoth and Leviathan. Job answers him, the LORD rebukes the three friends for not speaking rightly of him as Job did, and Job's fortunes are restored twice over.

Job is the Bible's deepest look at undeserved suffering and one of its hardest books to translate. It asks whether anyone serves God for nothing, whether the world runs on justice, and how a person in pain may speak to God. Jews and Christians have read it as the true story of a patient saint, as a parable, as a drama of protest, and as a book that leaves the reasons with God. This site translates it from the Hebrew, marks where the meaning is uncertain, and gives the main readings side by side.
facts: Not named. The Talmud says Moses wrote it (Bavli Bava Batra 14b–15a); the same passage records teachers who placed Job in the days of the patriarchs, the judges, the kingdom or the return from exile, and one who said Job never lived and the book is a parable (15a). Most scholars think an unknown Israelite poet of great skill wrote the poetry, perhaps reworking an older story about a righteous man named Job, whom Ezekiel 14:14 already names beside Noah and Daniel.

The story is set in a world like that of the patriarchs: wealth counted in flocks, Job offering sacrifices for his own family (1:5), a life of 140 years after his trials (42:16). Traditional views date the writing to the time of Moses or of Solomon. Most scholars date it between the 600s and the 300s BC, many to the 500s or 400s BC, in or after the Babylonian exile, because of its language, its Accuser (compare Zechariah 3:1–2) and its links with Isaiah 40–55, Jeremiah and Lamentations. Copies at Qumran, one in the old Hebrew script, an Aramaic translation (11QtgJob) and the Greek translation of the 100s BC show it was long established by then.

The land of Uz (1:1), probably in Edom or north Arabia, east and southeast of Israel (Lamentations 4:21; Genesis 36:28), and the court of heaven (1:6–12; 2:1–6). Job and his friends are not Israelites: Eliphaz comes from Teman in Edom, Bildad is a Shuhite and Zophar a Naamathite (2:11).

A prose story (1–2; 42:7–17) frames a long poem (3:1–42:6): a curse and laments, three rounds of debate, a poem on wisdom (28), an oath of innocence (31), the speeches of Elihu (32–37) and the speeches of the LORD from the storm (38–41). It belongs with Proverbs and Ecclesiastes among the Bible's wisdom books.

Hebrew, the hardest in the Bible. Job has more words found nowhere else in Scripture than any other book, many Aramaic-sounding forms, and some words best explained from Arabic or Ugaritic. Its names for God are mostly El, Eloah and Shaddai ("the Almighty"); the name YHWH ("the LORD") appears in the prose frame and the divine speeches, almost never in the debate.

42 chapters, 1,070 verses. The Old Greek translation is about one sixth shorter than the Hebrew; Origen filled its gaps from the Greek of Theodotion, marking them with asterisks. In Hebrew Bibles the speeches of the LORD on Leviathan are numbered 40:25–41:26 (English 41:1–34).
authorship: The Talmud says "Moses wrote his own book, the section of Balaam, and Job" (Bavli Bava Batra 14b), and many Jewish and Christian readers have followed it, or have credited Job himself, Elihu or Solomon. On this view Job lived in the age of the patriarchs, as his long life, his priestly role in his family and his wealth in flocks suggest, and the book preserves a true history that Israel received early. Some conservative scholars today hold that the events are historical and ancient while leaving the date of writing open, perhaps in Solomon's time, when wisdom writing flourished (1 Kings 4:29–34).

Most scholars think an unknown Israelite poet composed the dialogue and set it within an older prose story about a righteous man named Job (compare Ezekiel 14:14). Dates proposed range from the 600s to the 300s BC; many prefer the 500s or 400s, because of the book's Aramaic-colored Hebrew, its figure of the Accuser (Zechariah 3; compare 1 Chronicles 21:1), its apparent use of Jeremiah 20:14–18 and its kinship with Isaiah 40–55 and Lamentations. Many think the speeches of Elihu (32–37), who is not mentioned before or after, were added by a later writer, and some think the same of the poem on wisdom (28). The disordered third round (24–27) is usually explained as damage or rearrangement in copying.

Other scholars, among them Gordis, Andersen, Habel and Janzen, defend the book as a planned whole: the prose and poetry need each other, Elihu prepares for the divine speeches, and the broken third round shows the friends running out of arguments. Carol Newsom has argued that the book deliberately sets different voices and forms side by side, so that its unity is a debate rather than a single message.

audience.to: Israelites who had lived through disaster, most likely Judeans in the Babylonian exile or in the generations after it (the 500s and 400s BC): people who had lost land, city, Temple, king and children, and who had been taught that God blesses the righteous and punishes the wicked (Deuteronomy 28; Proverbs 3:1–10). The book was probably shaped and copied by Israel's wise men and scribes, the same circles that kept Proverbs. Yet it tells of a man who was not an Israelite, in a land outside Israel, in a distant past, so that it speaks to any human being who suffers.
audience.why: To test the common teaching about reward and punishment by placing a man of proven goodness in the worst suffering, and to ask whether people serve God only for what he gives them (1:9). It gives sufferers words for lament and protest that God in the end does not condemn, warns comforters against defending God with false charges against the suffering, and sets human wisdom before the freedom and greatness of the Creator. Knowing that the first readers had suffered as a people changes the reading: the friends' answers were Israel's own answers, Job's complaints were Israel's own complaints (compare Lamentations 3 and Psalm 44), and the double restoration of 42:10 would have sounded like the hope of Isaiah 40:2 and 61:7.
views: Many scholars read Job as a response to the catastrophe of 586 BC and its aftermath, written in the 500s or 400s BC for Judeans asking whether God was just and whether faith was still possible (Newsom, for example, places the book in the Persian period).

Others date the dialogue to the 600s BC, before the fall of Jerusalem, when Assyrian and Babylonian power pressed on Judah and the teaching of Proverbs and Deuteronomy was being questioned; Pope and Hartley favor a seventh-century date.

Some stress a setting among sages and scribes who taught the wisdom of Proverbs: Job questions that teaching from the inside, for students who knew it well. On this view the book need not answer one national disaster but the perennial problem of the righteous sufferer (Clines).
Israel in the time of Moses or Solomon

Traditional Jewish and Christian readers who follow the Talmud's view that Moses wrote Job (Bava Batra 15a) see it as given to Israel early, perhaps in the wilderness, as comfort and instruction; others link it with the wisdom of Solomon's court. On these views the patriarchal setting is the real date of the events (Andersen weighs these views and leaves the date open).

Many readers, ancient and modern, stress that the book's hero, setting and names for God are deliberately not Israelite, so that its first audience is in effect anyone who suffers. Maimonides read it as a parable addressed to all who think about providence (Guide 3.22–23).

lenses.name: History as told
lenses.desc: Many Jewish and Christian readers take Job as a real man of the distant past, from the land of Uz, whose trials happened as told; Ezekiel 14:14 and James 5:11 name him beside Noah and Daniel and as a model of endurance. The Talmud records the debate: one rabbi says 'Job never existed; he is a parable', and others place him in the time of Moses, Jacob or the return from exile (Bava Batra 15a–b).

lenses.name: Critical
lenses.desc: Most scholars see a prose frame (1–2, 42:7–17), perhaps an older folk tale, around a long poem of debate written by a gifted poet, usually dated between the 600s and 300s BC. They debate whether the Elihu speeches (32–37) and the poem on wisdom (28) were added later, and why the third round of speeches (24–27) seems broken.

lenses.name: Ancient wisdom
lenses.desc: Job belongs to a family of ancient Near Eastern writings about why the righteous suffer: the Babylonian 'I Will Praise the Lord of Wisdom' (Ludlul bel nemeqi) and 'Babylonian Theodicy', the Egyptian 'Dispute of a Man with His Ba', and a Sumerian 'Man and His God'. Reading them beside Job shows what is shared and what is new.

lenses.name: Jewish tradition
lenses.desc: The rabbis argue over Job: a righteous gentile or an Israelite; a saint, or a man who 'did not sin with his lips' but did 'in his heart' (Rava, Bava Batra 16a). Rashi and Ibn Ezra read his complaints closely, and Maimonides (Guide 3.22–23) reads the book as a parable about providence, each speaker standing for a school of thought. Job is one of the few books that may be studied on the fast of the Ninth of Av.

lenses.name: Christian
lenses.desc: Christians read Job as a lesson in patient endurance (James 5:11), an honest prayer book for suffering, and a book that leaves the cause of suffering with God. Many hear 'I know that my redeemer lives' (19:25) as pointing to Christ and the resurrection, as Handel's Messiah does; others read it as Job's hope for vindication in this life. Gregory the Great's 'Moralia on Job' is a classic of Christian reading.

sections.b:
The text page beside each chapter can show several translations. Only the one you pick is loaded.

Plain English Translation

A fresh rendering made for this site from the Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex), at about an 8th-grade reading level. Each verse was drafted from a word-by-word gloss of the Hebrew, then checked against other English versions and redrafted wherever it followed one of them too closely. Job is mostly poetry: the Plain English Translation keeps one verse per line, marks the poetic lines with slashes, and tries to keep parallel lines parallel and short. Headings mark each change of speaker. Where the Hebrew is uncertain, which in Job is often, the Plain English Translation gives the most likely sense and the notes give the main alternatives, from the Greek, the Targum, the Vulgate and modern study of related languages.

Key terms

Ha-satan is "the Accuser," a title, not a name (see 1:6). Shaddai is "the Almighty." El, Eloah and Elohim are all "God"; YHWH is "the LORD." Tam of a person is "wholehearted" and tummah "integrity"; hesed is "loyal love"; She'ol is left as "Sheol." At 1:5, 1:11, 2:5 and 2:9 the Hebrew writes "bless" for "curse"; the Plain English Translation gives the meaning, "curse," and a note explains. On the go'el of 19:25, see the note there.

The text and the versions

The Plain English Translation follows the Leningrad Codex. Readings of the Old Greek are cited from Rahlfs' edition, much of it checked at the Blue Letter Bible's Septuagint pages, with Claude Cox's English in NETS; the Qumran Aramaic Targum (11QtgJob) from its official edition; the rabbinic Targum from Mangan's translation. In Hebrew Bibles the end of chapter 40 and chapter 41 are numbered differently: Hebrew 40:25–41:26 is English 41:1–34, and this site uses the English numbers.

Other translations

The Berean Standard Bible, the King James Version, the American Standard Version, Young's Literal Translation and the World English Bible can be shown for comparison.

Job is built like a great arch, with a prose story at each end and poetry in between.

The prose frame (1–2; 42:7–17). A simple, repetitive tale: two scenes in heaven, two tests on earth, the arrival of three friends, and at the end the LORD's verdict and Job's restoration.

The opening lament (3). Job curses his day and longs for death.

Three rounds of debate (4–27). In each round Eliphaz, Bildad and Zophar speak in turn and Job answers each one: round one 4–14, round two 15–21, round three 22–27. As the rounds go on, the friends move from comfort to accusation, and Job from despair to a demand for a hearing with God.

The broken third round (22–27). The third round does not keep the pattern. Bildad's speech is only six verses (25), Zophar does not speak at all, and Job says things in 24:18–24 and 27:13–23 that sound like the friends' views. Some scholars rearrange the chapters to restore a speech for Zophar and a longer one for Bildad; others read the breakdown as deliberate: the friends have nothing left to say, or Job is quoting them.

The poem on wisdom (28). A calm poem asks where wisdom can be found and answers that only God knows the way to it: "the fear of the Lord is wisdom" (28:28). Readers debate whether it is Job's voice, the narrator's, or an interlude.

Job's last defense (29–31). Job remembers his past honor (29), laments his present shame (30), and swears an oath of innocence (31), ending with a challenge for God to answer.

Elihu (32–37). A young man never mentioned before speaks four times, angry with both Job and the friends. He argues that God speaks through suffering to warn and save. No one answers him, and he is not mentioned at the end.

The divine speeches (38:1–42:6). The LORD answers Job from the windstorm in two speeches about creation and the wild animals, ending with Behemoth and Leviathan. Job replies briefly after each (40:3–5; 42:1–6).

The epilogue (42:7–17). The LORD tells the friends they did not speak rightly about him as Job did, Job prays for them, and his fortunes are doubled.

sections.h: The Hebrew of Job and why it is hard
sections.b:
Job is the hardest book of the Hebrew Bible to translate. Its poetry is compressed and allusive, and it uses more rare words than any other book: well over a hundred words appear only here or almost only here. Many forms look Aramaic, some words make sense only when compared with Arabic, Akkadian or Ugaritic, and the poet loves wordplay and double meanings. The text itself seems damaged in places, especially in chapters 24–27.

The difficulty was felt early. The Greek translators of the 100s BC often guessed, paraphrased or left lines out. The medieval commentator Abraham ibn Ezra thought the book had been translated into Hebrew from another language, which would explain its strangeness, and some modern scholars (N. H. Tur-Sinai) proposed an Aramaic original; most scholars reject this, but agree that the poet wrote a Hebrew rich in foreign color, perhaps to give his eastern characters an eastern voice. The Masoretes gave Job, Psalms and Proverbs a special system of poetic accents.

On this site the notes say where a line is uncertain and give the main proposals. Readers should expect that two careful translations of Job will often differ, and that both may be defensible.

sections.h: The Greek Job and the Qumran witnesses
sections.b:
The Old Greek. The first Greek translation of Job, made probably in the 100s BC, is about one sixth shorter than the Hebrew: roughly 400 of its lines are missing, especially in the speeches from chapter 21 on. The translator often abbreviated what he found repetitive or obscure, and he softened some of Job's harshest words about God. In the AD 200s Origen filled the gaps from the later Greek version of Theodotion and marked the added lines with asterisks; the Greek of most manuscripts, and of Rahlfs' edition, includes these asterisked lines (see Gentry). The shorter Old Greek survives in the Sahidic Coptic translation. The Greek also adds two long passages: a speech of Job's wife at 2:9 (see the variant there) and an ending after 42:17 that identifies Job with Jobab, king of Edom (Genesis 36:33), and says he will rise again. A Jewish writer named Aristeas, known only through quotations by Alexander Polyhistor in Eusebius, had already identified Job with Jobab by the first century BC.

Qumran. The Dead Sea Scrolls include small Hebrew fragments of Job from Caves 2 and 4, one of them written in the old Hebrew script, a sign of how ancient the book was thought to be. They also include two Aramaic translations: a small one from Cave 4 (4QtgJob) and a large one from Cave 11 (11QtgJob), which covers parts of chapters 17 to 42 and ends at 42:11. The Talmud tells that Rabban Gamaliel the Elder ordered a Targum of Job to be hidden away (Bavli Shabbat 115a), proof that such translations existed in the first century.

The rabbinic Targum and the Vulgate. The later rabbinic Targum of Job, an Aramaic paraphrase that sometimes gives two explanations of a verse, and Jerome's Latin Vulgate, made from the Hebrew about AD 400, are important witnesses to how the text was understood.

In Job 1–2 "the satan" (ha-satan) is one of the sons of God who come before the LORD. The Hebrew word means adversary or accuser, and the article shows it is a title. He roams the earth, questions whether Job's piety is "for no reason" (1:9), and receives permission to test Job within limits. After 2:7 he disappears.

Readers have understood him in three main ways. A loyal officer of the heavenly court, a prosecutor or inspector like the Persian king's "eyes," who tests on God's behalf: so many Jewish readers (the Talmud says he "acted for the sake of heaven," Bava Batra 16a) and most modern scholars, who note that the Hebrew Bible develops a personal devil only late (compare 1 Chronicles 21:1). The devil, God's enemy, malicious but bound: so most Christian readers from Gregory the Great to Calvin, reading Job with Revelation 12:9–10 and 1 Peter 5:8, and the Greek translators, who called him ho diabolos. A story figure who gives voice to the reader's suspicion that goodness is only self-interest. Whichever view is taken, the book is clear that the Accuser cannot act without the LORD's word and that the LORD, not the Accuser, has the last word.

sections.h: Why the righteous suffer: the book's answer
sections.b:
Job does not give one neat answer to the problem of suffering, but it gives several partial ones and rejects one.

The prologue gives the reader a reason Job never learns: his suffering is a test of whether faith can be "for no reason" (1:9; 2:3). The point is not that every sufferer is being tested, but that suffering can have causes hidden from the sufferer and unrelated to sin.

The friends hold that God rewards the righteous and punishes the wicked, so that suffering points to sin and repentance brings restoration (4:7–8; 8:4–6; 11:13–19; 22:5). They also speak of discipline (5:17). The LORD says they did not speak rightly (42:7): the rule cannot be run backward from suffering to guilt.

Elihu stresses that God uses suffering to warn and to teach, to save people from pride and death (33:14–30; 36:8–15).

The divine speeches do not explain Job's suffering at all. They show Job a world far larger and wilder than any human scheme, governed by a God who sets limits on the sea, feeds the young lions and plays with Leviathan. Job is answered not with a reason but with a presence: "now my own eye has seen you" (42:5, see the note there).

The epilogue restores Job and declares that he, not his friends, spoke rightly about God, even though he complained bitterly.

Readings of the answer. Maimonides read the book as a parable of providence: Job's friends and Elihu stand for schools of thought, and Job learns that God's knowledge and care are unlike ours (Guide 3.22–23). Aquinas read it as a defense of providence that looks beyond this life to future reward. Gregory the Great and Calvin stressed God's hidden justice and the call to humble trust. Many modern readers find the book's honesty its answer: God accepts protest, and the comforters who defend him with false charges are rebuked. Others, such as Carl Jung in Answer to Job (1952), read the book as an indictment of God; Gustavo Gutiérrez read it as teaching both the language of contemplation and the language of prophecy, care for the suffering poor. The book leaves the reader with the question it began with: will we fear God for no reason?

sections.h: Job beside the ancient Near Eastern texts
sections.b:
Job was not the first ancient poem about a righteous sufferer. "I Will Praise the Lord of Wisdom" (Ludlul bel nemeqi), a Babylonian poem of the late second millennium BC, tells of a pious official who loses his position and health, is abandoned by family and friends, suffers terrible nights and finally is restored by Marduk, whom he praises. The Babylonian Theodicy (about 1000 BC), an acrostic poem, is a dialogue between a sufferer and a friend who defends the gods' justice and finally concedes that the gods made humans prone to lies. The Sumerian "A Man and His God" counsels a sufferer to confess unknown sins; the Egyptian "Dispute of a Man with His Ba" longs for death, and "The Eloquent Peasant" protests injustice at length. From Ugarit come the myths of Baal's battle with Yam and Litan (Leviathan) that Job's poetry uses.

What is shared: the righteous sufferer, the friend's dialogue, the lament over nights and illness, the sense that the gods' ways are beyond knowing, and a final restoration. What is new in Job: the prologue that tells the reader the sufferer is innocent; the sustained, legal protest against God himself; the friends' rebuke; and a God who answers in person, not with an explanation but with creation. Most scholars think Job knew this wider tradition, though no direct borrowing from a single text can be shown.

In the Hebrew Bible Job belongs to the third division, the Writings (Ketuvim). The Talmud's list orders the first Writings Ruth, Psalms, Job, Proverbs (Bavli Bava Batra 14b), and the great medieval manuscripts, the Leningrad and Aleppo codices, have Psalms, Job, Proverbs, after Chronicles. Some lists differ: many printed Hebrew Bibles put Proverbs before Job, and Greek manuscripts vary, Codex Vaticanus placing Job after the Song of Songs. Latin Bibles from Jerome on put Job first among the poetical books, before Psalms, an order Christian Bibles still follow, partly because Job was thought to have lived in the age of the patriarchs. Job, Proverbs and Psalms share the Masoretes' special poetic accents and are known together by the first letters of their Hebrew names as sifre emet, "the books of truth."

Job's place in Scripture was not seriously disputed in Judaism or the early church, though readers argued about its history and its hero. It is among the few books that Jewish custom allows to be studied on the fast of the Ninth of Av, a day of mourning. Orthodox churches read the Greek Job, with its longer speech of Job's wife and its ending after 42:17, and honor Job as a saint.

Job has long been read aloud in the churches, especially at funerals and in seasons of mourning. The traditional Catholic Office of the Dead read nine lessons from Job, and the Catholic funeral Lectionary offers Job 19:1, 23–27; on Sundays Job 7:1–4, 6–7 is read in Year B (Fifth Sunday in Ordinary Time). Orthodox churches read the Greek Job at Vespers in the first days of Holy Week and keep the feast of Job "the much-suffering" on May 6. The burial service of the Book of Common Prayer (1662) opens with John 11:25, then Job 19:25–27, then 1 Timothy 6:7 with Job 1:21. The Revised Common Lectionary, used by many Lutheran, Methodist, Anglican and Reformed churches, reads Job in sequence on four Sundays of Year B (Propers 22–25). In Judaism, Job is one of the few books that may be studied on the Ninth of Av, and the burial prayer Tziduk ha-Din quotes Job 1:21.

spec.title: Claude's theory: two silences
spec.body: My own reading: the book is framed by two silences. At the start the friends sit with Job for seven days without a word, "for they could see how terrible his pain was" (2:13). At the end, after the LORD speaks, Job puts his hand over his mouth (40:4–5). The first silence is the right response to a sufferer; the second is the right response to God. In between, everyone talks: the friends to explain God, Job to accuse and to plead. The friends' trouble begins when they break their silence to explain; Job's peace comes when he stops explaining and sees. Commentators often praise the friends' first silence and discuss Job's later one; pairing them as the book's frame and its lesson about speech is my suggestion.

Wide horizontal composition, 3:2.

The fullest modern commentary, with exhaustive notes on the Hebrew and the history of interpretation.

traditions.q: Is the book of Job history?
views: The Church does not require one answer. Following Divino Afflante Spiritu's call to attend to literary forms, many Catholic scholars read Job as an inspired teaching story built around a traditional figure; older Catholic tradition, from Gregory the Great and Aquinas, took Job as a real man whose words were set down in poetic form.
Job is honored as a real saint, 'the righteous and much-suffering Job,' with a feast on May 6, and the Greek ending of Job, which names his family and land, is read as part of the book.
Luther is reported to have held that Job is a true history, but that a gifted writer shaped it like a play, so that not every word was spoken as written (Table Talk).

Most hold that Job was a historical person, pointing to Ezekiel 14:14 and James 5:11, while accepting that the speeches are crafted poetry; some evangelical scholars allow that the book may be a parable without denying its inspiration.
Job is a true account of a real man, written, they hold, by Moses.
